document.title: Pakistan Support for Taliban (State 185645)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
document.note: [Secret] State calls the magnitude of recent Pakistani support for the Taliban unprecedented. It instructs the Embassy to confront Pakistan over reports of materiel, fuel, funding, technical assistance, advisers and Pakistani nationals fighting for the Taliban. Cited in The 9/11 Commission Report, ch. 6 fn. 68.

events.description: Albright's opening statement at Six-Plus-Two meeting calling for ceasefire and negotiations.
State Department cable instructing Embassy Islamabad to raise concerns on Pakistani support for Taliban.
Albright asked Kofi Annan to send Vendrell back to the region; Sattar agreed.
Albright delivered opening statement at the Six-Plus-Two meeting calling for a cease-fire and negotiations without preconditions, and said the Taliban had failed international standards.
At the Six Plus Two meeting Albright asked Annan to send Vendrell back to the region; Pakistani FM Sattar agreed.
State Department sent action cable 185645 to Embassy Islamabad directing the Charge/Ambassador to raise concerns about Pakistani support for the Taliban.
Large numbers of Pakistani nationals reportedly moved into Afghanistan to fight for the Taliban with tacit Pakistani government acquiescence.

sources_cited: Secretary Albright statements at Six Plus Two meeting, New York, 15 Sep 2000
US intelligence reports on Pakistani support to Taliban (unspecified)
key_claims: The US assessed that Pakistani support for the Taliban's military campaign was unprecedented in magnitude in 2000.
Pakistan was reported to supply the Taliban with materiel, fuel, funding, technical assistance and military advisors.
Large numbers of Pakistani nationals reportedly moved into Afghanistan to fight for the Taliban with tacit government acquiescence.
The US feared the Taliban might use Pakistani territory to outflank Northern Alliance positions.
The US would not accept a Taliban military victory and argued it would not bring recognition or a UN seat.
The US did not see Masood as the answer and favored a broader UN-facilitated peace process involving Vendrell.
